articles.body: The author Lois McMaster Bujold has said that “the writer should always reserve the right to come up with a better idea.” That's a useful guideline for any reader to keep in mind. articles.body: Everything I post here goes out through blog-kit : a small publisher for the dev.to API, a diagram renderer, and a cover maker. The bit I wouldn't post without is the leak check. My drafts start life full of real addresses and hostnames from my notes, and one slipping into a public post is the kind of mistake you only make once. Five minutes to set up, and the guide is run on a fresh Ubuntu machine every week. Dry run Python 3 and the standard library, that's it. git clone https://github.com/casareanderson/blog-kit.git && cd blog-kit python3 publish.py drafts/devto-05-buzzwords.md It prints the title, tags and word count and ends with dry run — nothing sent. Add --publish when you mean it. Every run is a dry run unless you say otherwise. No key needed.

articles.title: AI Coding Assistants and Productivity: What the Research Actually Says
articles.excerpt: Originally published on shipfastdev.com. The research on AI coding assistants does not give one number. Controlled experiments on well-defined tasks show large speedups (55% faster in GitHub's 2022 st…
articles.body: Originally published on shipfastdev.com . The research on AI coding assistants does not give one number. Controlled experiments on well-defined tasks show large speedups (55% faster in GitHub's 2022 study), field experiments in companies show a smaller but real gain (about 26% more completed tasks), and the best-known randomised trial on experienced developers working in their own large codebases found they were 19% slower with AI. At team level, Google's DORA research finds more throughput but less stability. Here is what each major study measured, why they disagree, and how to use the evidence when you plan a roadmap or judge a developer's estimates.

articles.title: AWS Puts the Region Inside the AS Path on Direct Connect
articles.excerpt: TL;DR AWS BYOASN is a feature of Amazon VPC IP Address Manager that lets a provider bring its own public Autonomous System Number to AWS and attach a different one to each Region. AWS published the wa…
articles.body: TL;DR AWS BYOASN is a feature of Amazon VPC IP Address Manager that lets a provider bring its own public Autonomous System Number to AWS and attach a different one to each Region. AWS published the walkthrough on 3 November 2026, combining BYOIP, VPC IPAM and BYOASN on Direct Connect public virtual interfaces. The problem it answers is identifying the regional origin of routes at a Direct Connect location: a Zurich circuit associated with the Frankfurt Region advertises prefixes from a different regulatory jurisdiction. Filtering by IP prefix fails on two counts, because providers keep per-Region prefix mappings internal and reallocation forces coordinated edits on the customer's routers.

articles.title: Three.js on mobile - the device gotchas that tank a configurator
articles.excerpt: A configurator that runs at a locked 60 on your laptop can be a stuttering mess on a customer's phone, and the profiler on your desktop will not show you why. The causes are device realities, not bugs…
articles.body: A configurator that runs at a locked 60 on your laptop can be a stuttering mess on a customer's phone, and the profiler on your desktop will not show you why. The causes are device realities, not bugs in your render loop. Here are the four that catch people. 1. Pixel ratio will quietly 3x your work Phones report a devicePixelRatio of 2, 3, even 4. Pass that straight to the renderer and you are rendering nine times the pixels of a ratio-1 screen, for no visible gain on a product shot. Cap it: renderer . setPixelRatio ( Math . min ( window . devicePixelRatio , 2 )) This single line is the most common reason a configurator goes from slideshow to smooth on mobile. 2. GPU memory is small, and textures eat it first A mid-range phone has a fraction of the GPU memory of a laptop.

articles.title: My Next.js articles shipped inside a hidden div, and nothing warned me
articles.excerpt: My pages looked fine in a browser. Google was indexing them. Then I read the HTML the way a crawler reads it, with no JavaScript: curl -s https://your-site.com/some-page -A 'OAI-SearchBot/1.0' There w…
articles.body: My pages looked fine in a browser. Google was indexing them. Then I read the HTML the way a crawler reads it, with no JavaScript: curl -s https://your-site.com/some-page -A 'OAI-SearchBot/1.0' There was a header, an empty slot and a footer. The article came after the footer, inside <div hidden id="S:1"> . A small inline script moves it into the slot when the page loads. Googlebot runs that script. A crawler that doesn't run JavaScript gets a hidden block at the bottom of the page. I can't see inside every crawler to know what it does with that. I didn't want to bet my pages on it.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
articles.excerpt: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
articles.body: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security. The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats. We regret to inform you...

articles.title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.
